Senses.PreferredTarget: take the road and return home
AlternateTargets: return home by way of the road
Senses.Explanation: Literally, “take the road and return home.” The Zen bend is visible in the corpus's repeated reversals and pairings: the phrase is a stock Chan verdict for a person's handling of what is already under discussion, yet the records deny that its homeward journey is an ordinary change of location. One record says that even if someone speaks of “turning back with mastery and taking the road home,” it is “a thousand miles and ten thousand miles” away (回途得妙，就路還家，便是千里萬里). Another sets “take the road and return home” against “leave home and take the road” (離家就路), then says that leaving does not move an inch and returning has no bodily image. Wuyi Yuanlai explicitly pairs it with “turn around and return to the father” (轉身歸父). Shiyu Mingfang applies the phrase three times to actual travel stages—leaving Jinze by boat, passing Jiaxing and Chongde, and reaching Fojih monastery—so the literal journey remains available inside the stock expression. Juelang Sheng calls “responding to the occasion and benefiting beings; taking the road and returning home” (因機利物，就路還家) the staff-bearer's ordinary occupation, alongside “meeting conditions and acting as host” (遇緣作主) as his own-house style. The corpus therefore bends a homeward-road idiom into a recurring Chan appraisal while also recording literal journeys and explicit counter-journeys.
Senses.Note: No single master-specific sense is warranted. The phrase occurs across many late records, often with “turn around and return to the father” or the reversed “leave home and take the road.” The article reports those textual relations without assigning a spiritual force to “home.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 直饒說箇回途得妙，就路還家，便是千里萬里。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Complete Book of the Five Lamps, Shiyu Mingfang section; the text itself denies that merely saying the homeward formula is arrival.

Occurrences.Kwic: 離金澤，跨船舷，也是就路還家；過嘉興，由崇德，也是就路還家；到塘棲，入佛日，登戒錄，要羯磨，也是就路還家。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Shiyu's record applies the phrase repeatedly to named legs of a literal journey. The roster does not supply a securely matched canonical link for this section, so MasterName remains null.

Occurrences.Kwic: 此是故鄉景象，若肯就路還家，便得轉身歸父。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Wuyi Yuanlai's Extended Record, sermon at Boshan Nengren monastery; an exact pairing with “turn around and return to the father.”

Occurrences.Kwic: 一人就路還家，一人離家就路。離家就路，寸步不曾移；就路還家，通身無影像。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Ancient Snow Zhe's Recorded Sayings, Cuiyan monastery section; the text draws the full return/leave contrast and supplies the no-movement and no-image predicates.

Occurrences.Kwic: 因機利物，就路還家，此是杖人尋常活計；到處稱尊，遇緣作主，此是杖人本分宗風。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Juelang Sheng's Recorded Sayings; the phrase is explicitly classified as the staff-bearer's ordinary occupation and paired with meeting conditions as host.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, flourishing or luxuriant (鬱鬱) yellow flowers (黃花): "flourishing yellow flowers." The phrase occurs 57 times in 41 allowlisted texts. Its distinctively Chan deployment is the frequently quoted proposition, "the green bamboo is entirely the body of the teaching; the flourishing yellow flowers are nothing other than wisdom" (青青翠竹，盡是法身；鬱鬱黃花，無非般若). The fuller exact yellow-flower formula occurs 18 times in 17 texts, while "green bamboo" (青青翠竹) occurs 116 times in 68. The records preserve disagreement rather than a single unopposed gloss. A question to National Teacher Huizhong says that some call the proposition an erroneous saying while others trust it as inconceivable; his recorded answer accepts it by placing bamboo and flowers within the range of the teaching body and wisdom. The same transmitted passage then has a Huayan lecturer ask Dazhu Huihai why he does not permit the formula; Dazhu distinguishes appearing in response to bamboo and flowers from wisdom or the teaching body being located in those objects. Later, Shending Yikui rebukes people who hear the formula, hold rigidly to it, and never shift at all, calling a fitting phrase "a donkey-tethering stake for ten thousand ages" (一句合頭語，萬劫繫驢橛). In another exchange he asks how wisdom is understood when the yellow flowers are right here, and tells the respondent that he has let the yellow flowers down. Chan thus bends a scene of colored plants into a portable, disputed proposition and a live examination question; this entry reports the acceptance, distinction, and correction recorded by the texts without deciding among them.
Senses.Note: The fixed pair with green bamboo is lexicographically central. Other hits use the flowers literally in autumn poems; those ordinary deployments do not establish an additional Chan sense.

Occurrences.Kwic: 僧問忠國師：『青青翠竹，盡是法身；鬱鬱黃花，無非般若。有人不許，云是邪說；亦有信者，云不思議。不知若為？』
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Jinming Jin quotes a question to National Teacher Huizhong that explicitly records opposed assessments of the bamboo-and-yellow-flower proposition.

Occurrences.Kwic: 禪師何故不許青青翠竹盡是法身，鬱鬱黃花無非般若？』珠云：『法身無象，應翠竹以成形；般若無知，對黃花而顯相。非彼黃花翠竹而有般若法身
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The quoted Dazhu Huihai exchange distinguishes manifestation in response to flowers and bamboo from locating wisdom or the teaching body in those objects.

Occurrences.Kwic: 見說青青翠竹無非法身、鬱鬱黃花無非般若，一據據定，更不移易絲毫。殊不知，一句合頭語，萬劫繫驢橛。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Shending Yikui criticizes rigid adherence to the stock line and calls a fitting phrase a donkey-tethering stake for ten thousand ages.

Occurrences.Kwic: 師問眾：「鬱鬱黃花無非般若花，在此作麼生會般若？」品維那云：「從來不眼花。」師云：「辜負黃花也。」
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Shending turns the formula into a question with the flowers present and rejects the officer's reply as letting the flowers down.

Occurrences.Kwic: 問。青青翠竹。盡是真如。鬱鬱黃花。無非般若。如何是般若。師曰。黃泉無老少。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: In Jiuxian Yuxian's section, the formula supplies the premise for 'what is wisdom?' and the master answers, 'at the Yellow Springs there is neither old nor young.'
